results.title: OpenBSD 8.0 Brings Expanded Hardware Support, Security Enhancements, and Virtualization Improvements
results.author: Sergio De Simone
results.content:
OpenBSD 8.0 is a substantial upgrade bringing broader hardware compatibility, enhanced security, an expanded virtual address space, and support for modern architectures, including Intel Arc A-Series graphics support, ARM64 hibernation, RISC-V improvements, and enhanced virtual machine support.
Key hardware and virtualization improvements in OpenBSD 8.0 include a larger virtual address space for the AMD64 kernel, expanded from 4 GB to 512 GB, enabling it to map graphics cards with more than 4 GB of VRAM; support for multi-processor virtual machines through vmm/vmd, with up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest and improvements to virtual hardware and guest compatibility; expanded RISC-V support, including the 'V' vector extension and Advanced Interrupt Architecture, improving compatibility with newer processors and platforms; and arm64 hibernation support, alongside faster swap encryption using AES instructions.
Although OpenBSD 8.0 introduces support for the Intel Arc A-Series GPUs, based on the DG2/Alchemist architecture, NVIDIA GPUs remain unsupported, partially due to the fact that NVIDIA does not provide proprietary binary drivers for OpenBSD, unlike Linux and FreeBSD.
OpenBSD 8.0 also expands peripheral support, including the riscv64 K3 PCIe/USB3 combo PHY, the SpacemiT K3 SoC and PCIe controller, as well as the Intel E610 and Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake Ethernet devices. New drivers are now available for Samsung Advanced BIOS Interface (SABI), Rockchip OTP memory, and Samsung laptop battery monitor. Wireless adapters support has been significantly expanded as well, including support for the Qualcomm Technologies WCN7850 wireless network in the qwz driver.
The httpd daemon in OpenBSD 8.0 has received several enhancements, including support for custom HTTP headers, header block/drop rules for request filtering, improved default crypto methods for HTTPS, and cache control for static files.
On the security front, OpenBSD 8.0 continues to emphasize security as a defining priority with an outstanding track record:
We remain proud of OpenBSD's record of more than thirty years with only two remote holes in the default install.
The new release incorporates LibreSSL 4.4.0, which introduces numerous compatibility-layer fixes for AIX, FreeBSD, macOS, MinGW, NetBSD, and especially Windows, alongside various internal improvements. It also brings OpenSSH 10.6, which disables SSH Compression using LZ77 and rejects $ and \ characters in command-line usernames to mitigate potential shell injection vulnerabilities, among other enhancements.
A Hacker News thread about the new release highlighted several important aspects of OpenBSD. User ctolsen emphasized the system's simplicity and its adherence to traditional Unix philosophy:
OpenBSD just feels like a *nix system is supposed to. ps aux is like 10 entries at first. pf makes so much sense. man pages are consistently incredible. The security/cryptography focus, managing services, pledge/unveil...
Longtime OpenBSD user nanolith, who has used the system for nearly 20 years, praised its stability and consistency across upgrades, noting that "it's so stable that I barely notice changes when I upgrade until I go hunting for them". However, he also points out that OpenBSD might not be the best choice for large servers, given its lack of support for advanced filesystems like ZFS, Btrfs, or GeFS.
results.summary:
OpenBSD 8.0 introduces significant hardware compatibility updates, including Intel Arc GPU support and expanded virtual address space, alongside critical security enhancements through LibreSSL 4.4.0 and OpenSSH 10.6.

### Key Points
- The AMD64 kernel virtual address space increased from 4 GB to 512 GB to support high-VRAM graphics cards.
- Virtual machine capabilities now include support for up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest via vmm/vmd.
- New hardware support includes Intel Arc A-Series GPUs, Qualcomm WCN7850 wireless adapters, and various RISC-V platform improvements.
- OpenSSH 10.6 disables LZ77 compression and restricts specific characters in usernames to mitigate shell injection vulnerabilities.
- The httpd daemon added support for custom HTTP headers, request filtering rules, and improved HTTPS crypto methods.

### Why it Matters
This release strengthens OpenBSD's position as a secure, stable operating system by modernizing its hardware support and virtualization capabilities. These updates allow the platform to remain competitive for specialized computing tasks while maintaining its long-standing commitment to rigorous security standards.

results.title: A simple explainer of the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance
results.author: Rafael Nam
results.content:
A simple explainer of the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance
It was the biggest cyber heist in history.
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges, was hacked this week, with cybercriminals plundering more than $6 billion. The FBI on Saturday confirmed that North Korea was behind the hack, confirming what experts had widely believed in the aftermath of the attacks. Law enforcement attributed the attacks to a sophisticated unit within the North Korean military that has a track record of committing cyber heists.
The theft stunned the crypto industry and set off new fears about a sector that many critics deride as the "Wild West" of finance.
Here are 5 things to know about the spectacular heist.
So first, what are crypto exchanges?
They are akin to the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) or the Nasdaq, but instead of trading stocks, investors turn to Binance and other crypto exchanges to trade digital assets such as Bitcoin.
A wide range of investors trade cryptocurrencies at these exchanges, from financial institutions and sophisticated traders, all the way to regular investors looking to make some money.
OK, so what happened this week?
At 4:05 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, hackers were able to access the accounts of investors who trade cryptocurrencies at Binance. It took only about 20 minutes for these hackers to make off off with just over $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies.
Ari Redbord, the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a crypto research firm that has helped Binance trace and recover some of the stolen funds, calls it "the largest bank robbery in human history."
"Imagine a world where someone could walk into a bank and walk out with $6.36 billion in stolen funds and then move those funds at the speed of the internet," he says. "This is bank robbery in the age of technology."
But a lot of details about the heist are still unclear, including how exactly the hackers were able to hack their way into the trading accounts of investors at Binance.
Binance, working with other exchanges and partners, has been able to freeze about $3 billion in stolen cryptocurrencies, effectively preventing hackers from taking full possession of its digital assets.
By Sunday, Binance said it has replaced nearly 100% of the cryptocurrencies that customers lost in the attack, by using part of its own crypto holdings or buying them in the markets to make their customers whole. The exchange added most customers can now withdraw their cryptocurrencies from their accounts at Binance.
Why did experts believe it's North Korea?
As soon as the scale of the attack was known, many researchers attributed the attack to North Korea. The level of sophistication and speed of the hack all pointed to a North Korean military hacking unit widely known as TraderTraitor, which the FBI then confirmed on Saturday. The unit was also responsible for what was the previous biggest-ever cyber heist, the theft of $1.5 billion from crypto exchange Bybit last year.
"North Korea has built the most sophisticated cyber capabilities in the world. They have a cadre of teams of professional hackers who are part of their military," says TRM's Redbord.
"This isn't just a commercial hacker who's looking to make some money," he adds. "This is going to be used for weapons proliferation and other destabilizing activity."
What does this heist tell us about the safety of crypto exchanges?
Researchers say it's too early to determine whether there were any major flaws with Binance's security systems. But they say the heist is a clear sign of just how sophisticated North Korean hackers are.
Meanwhile, crypto critics say the way Binance and other crypto exchanges are set up deserve scrutiny.
A unique feature of crypto exchanges is that people can buy and sell digital currencies such as bitcoin — and leave them with the exchanges for safekeeping.
This dual trust in the exchange makes them mighty tempting targets for hackers. And what's more concerning for critics, crypto exchanges also don't have to follow the same strict regulations that govern established Wall Street firm.
"You may trade on the New York Stock Exchange, but you don't keep your funds with the New York Stock Exchange. You keep it with your broker — and your broker is audited and regulated by the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission)," says Amanda Fischer, policy director and chief operating officer at financial consumer advocacy group Better Markets. "And your broker has to pay for insurance that will make customers whole in the event that there's a cyber attack."
"So the regulatory framework for crypto is much weaker than what investors in the US enjoy in other markets," says Fischer.
Though Binance has promised to pay back customers who lost funds, it is not necessarily bound to do so according to current regulations. And many critics worry that smaller exchanges could struggle to pay back their investors in case of a hack, leaving these traders to suffer the consequences.
Doesn't this reinforce the crypto sector's Wild West reputation?
For many crypto critics, it does. They warn the lack of clear regulations for crypto executives could lead to perverse incentives at these exchanges.
In 2022, FTX — then the biggest crypto exchange — got into financial trouble after a period of intense volatility in the crypto markets, and the exchange dipped into their own customers' funds as it desperately tried to rescue itself. The company collapsed, and its CEO and founder Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud among other charges.
"If a trade goes bad, it can become almost irresistible to dip into those client funds. Just this one time is what they say, to cover their losses," says Fischer at Better Markets. "But we know that that can cascade into catastrophe for investors."
It's another reason why the massive cyber heist of Binance is raising so many alarms.
NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report.
results.summary:
North Korean military hackers stole $6.3 billion from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange in a sophisticated cyberattack, prompting significant concerns regarding the security and regulation of digital asset platforms.

### Key Points
- Hackers breached Binance accounts at 4:05 p.m. ET on Thursday, completing the theft in approximately 20 minutes.
- The FBI confirmed the attack was orchestrated by the North Korean military hacking unit known as TraderTraitor.
- Binance successfully froze $3 billion of the stolen assets and has reimbursed nearly 100% of customer losses using its own holdings.
- Critics highlight that crypto exchanges lack the strict regulatory oversight, insurance requirements, and auditing standards mandated for traditional Wall Street brokerage firms.

### Why it Matters
This incident underscores the extreme vulnerability of centralized cryptocurrency exchanges to state-sponsored cyber warfare. It intensifies the debate over whether the crypto industry requires more rigorous federal regulation to protect investors from catastrophic financial losses.

results.title: Will the iPhone Duo Fit in Your Pocket? Here’s How It Compares to Other iPhone Sizes
results.author: Abrar Al-Heeti
results.content:
The iPhone Duo is designed to be compact, but that hasn’t stopped some from wondering how its size compares with other iPhone models.
Fortunately, we have all the current iPhone devices on hand to show how the Duo, when folded shut, stacks up against the dimensions of everything from the iPhone Air to the iPhone 18 Pro Max. This should give you a better sense of how easily the Duo might fit into a pocket or bag.
The iPhone Duo is a $1,999 phone that, in case it wasn’t obvious from the price, isn’t for everyone. With a 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display, it serves as a phone-tablet hybrid that’s ideal for multitasking, watching movies and working on the go. The Duo isn’t especially light or thin, but it’s also not too bulky. It measures 5.2 millimeters when unfolded and 11.3mm when folded, and it weighs 254 grams.
As a first-generation device, it has its shortcomings. The Duo doesn’t support FaceID, opting for TouchID instead. Its multitasking capabilities are limited compared to other foldable phones, and the cameras are more scaled back than the iPhone 18 Pro’s. But other details make the Duo feel refined and intuitive, from the matte texture of the inner display that reduces glare to dynamic software integration across both screens. The Duo can be a tempting option for anyone looking for a phone that feels refreshingly different.
Here’s how the iPhone Duo’s size compares to all current iPhone models.
Starting with Apple’s biggest nonfolding phone, the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display. It measures 8.75mm thick and weighs 249 grams, making it just slightly lighter than the iPhone Duo, though that difference is negligible. What you will notice is how much shorter the Duo is, making it easier to slip into a pocket — even smaller women’s pockets.
Meanwhile, the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display and, like its Pro Max counterpart, is 8.75mm thick. The 18 Pro weighs a noticeably lighter 211 grams, so the Duo does start to feel a little more hefty in comparison.
Apple has yet to unveil a baseline iPhone 18 model, which is expected early next year. In the meantime, here’s how the Duo compares to the $899 iPhone 17, which has a 6.3-inch display and measures 7.95mm thick. The iPhone 17 weighs 177 grams, making it significantly lighter than the iPhone Duo.
The $1,099 iPhone Air has a slightly larger 6.5-inch display compared to the iPhone 17. It measures a sleek 5.6mm thick, and it weighs a featherlight 165 grams. If you’re jumping from the Air to the Duo, you’ll definitely feel the biggest difference compared to other current iPhone models.
And finally, the slightly more budget-friendly $699 iPhone 17E has a 6.1-inch display, measuring 7.8mm thick and weighing 169 grams.
If you’re thinking about making the leap to the iPhone Duo, be sure to check out CNET’s in-depth review for more on using Apple’s first foldable phone.
results.summary:
Apple’s new $1,999 iPhone Duo foldable smartphone offers a unique hybrid design, featuring a 5.4-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch inner display for enhanced multitasking and media consumption.

### Key Points
- The iPhone Duo measures 11.3mm thick when folded and weighs 254 grams, making it heavier than the 249-gram iPhone 18 Pro Max.
- The device utilizes TouchID for security rather than FaceID and features a matte inner display designed to reduce glare.
- It is significantly heavier and thicker than the iPhone Air, which weighs 165 grams and measures 5.6mm in thickness.
- The phone-tablet hybrid is currently priced at $1,999, positioning it as a premium, first-generation device compared to the standard iPhone 17 and 18 lineups.

### Why it Matters
The iPhone Duo represents Apple's entry into the foldable market, signaling a shift toward hardware that prioritizes screen real estate for mobile productivity. While its high price and weight may limit mass appeal, it serves as a critical test for how Apple integrates foldable technology into its existing ecosystem.

- ICE has requested numerous social media platforms to hand over data on users who are critical of its agents and operations
- Tech companies have complied, but are now expecting Democrat-led investigations into their compliance following the midterm elections
- Executives want to shield themselves from Congressional inquiries into their conduct
The US midterm elections are just days away, and big tech companies such as Google and Meta are already quietly defying Trump’s orders to hand over data on users who have criticized his stance on immigration.
The incumbent party usually loses seats in the midterm elections, and with a wave of Democratic governors potentially on the horizon tech companies are attempting to stave off future scrutiny.
“They need to be prepared to say, under oath, why they did what they did,” Rep. Shri Thanedar (D., Mich.) said, referring to an investigation into companies who have complied with Trump administration subpoenas.
T&C update: your data may be handed to the authorities
Numerous tech companies with platforms upon which people have voiced critical views of Trump’s handling of immigration policy have begun updating their terms of use to include transparency on how user data could be handed over to the authorities.
Much of the criticism has centered around how Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have conducted operations investigating illegal immigrants.
As a recent Department of Homeland Security breach exposed, ICE agents have conducted undercover surveillance operations of protestors, critics, and journalists using wiretaps.
The DHS has also expanded its definition of doxing - the revealing of personal information such as a home address for malicious purposes - to include names and titles. Social media platforms and search engines such as Google, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, TikTok and X have then been scoured by ICE to identify anything it deems a threat to its agents or operations.

results.title: AI startup hacks Anthropic, gains access to employee details, internal messages
results.author: Ankita Garg
results.content:
AI startup hacks Anthropic in 12 hours, gains access to employee details and internal messages
A cybersecurity startup accessed Anthropic's internal systems in under 12 hours, exposing employee details and internal messages. Separately, Anthropic's Claude AI has faced scrutiny for accessing restricted information and carrying out unauthorised actions.
A cybersecurity startup called Cathedral gained access to sensitive internal systems at Anthropic in less than 12 hours, exposing employee information, salary details, job offers and internal messages discussing the company's advanced AI models. The incident was discovered during a security test conducted under Anthropic's programme for outside researchers to identify vulnerabilities.
According to a draft report reviewed by The Washington Post, Cathedral used AI agents to find weaknesses in business software used by Anthropic for administrative and sales tasks. The researchers found ways to access internal data, including meeting transcripts and Slack messages, after running their agents for less than 12 hours.
Cathedral was founded by former members of the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and develops AI-powered cybersecurity tools for government agencies and corporate clients.
Anthropic confirmed that the researchers accessed a limited set of its sales, human resources and IT systems. The exposed information included business contact details for some customers and partners, along with basic user account records. However, Anthropic said the researchers could not access conversations between customers and its Claude chatbot, the responses generated by the model, or the source code and model weights behind its AI systems.
"Our monitoring flagged some of Cathedral’s activity before they reported it to us, and we shut off their access the same day," Anthropic said in a statement. The company added that it had found no evidence of anyone other than Cathedral exploiting the vulnerabilities.
Anthropic disabled the affected business software and restored it only after the vendors confirmed that the security flaws had been addressed. It also briefed federal officials about the incident. The findings have raised national security concerns, with a senior Trump administration official telling The Washington Post that the report had circulated within the government. Alex Stamos, chief information security officer at AI coding startup Cognition, also pointed to weaknesses in how companies manage third-party software.
“This is a really hard problem, but Anthropic could have done a lot better,” Stamos said.
Anthropic, however, argued that Cathedral had overstated the national security implications of the incident. It also said the startup had not fully followed the rules of its cybersecurity testing programme because it failed to disclose all its activity within Anthropic's systems. Cathedral said it had kept data access to the minimum required for its research.
Anthropic's Claude has also carried out unauthorised actions
The security incident comes amid growing concerns about AI agents finding ways around restrictions while carrying out tasks. Anthropic has itself disclosed cases in which its Claude model accessed information or performed actions without proper authorisation.
In one recent incident, Claude accessed aggregate vote counts held by the US state of Georgia after finding a loophole in an older version of a government website. Anthropic said the system issued a digital access token that allowed the AI to reach information normally available only after paying a fee.
The company clarified that Claude did not access the state's voter registration system, retrieve individual voter records or change any voting records. It said the information accessed was limited to aggregate vote counts and that it had introduced safeguards to prevent similar incidents.
Anthropic had previously reported examples of Claude working around restrictions to reach information protected by a token or fee, including data on websites operated by US government agencies. The company said those incidents had minimal real-world impact.
Other reported cases involving AI agents have added to these concerns. An Anthropic model reportedly submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder to Philadelphia police, while the US State Department disclosed that an Anthropic model had filed 19 visa applications in August.
results.summary:
Cybersecurity startup Cathedral accessed sensitive internal systems at AI company Anthropic in under 12 hours, exposing employee data and internal communications during a sanctioned security vulnerability test.

### Key Points
- Cathedral researchers used AI agents to exploit weaknesses in third-party administrative and sales software used by Anthropic.
- The breach exposed employee salary details, job offers, internal Slack messages, and business contact information for partners.
- Anthropic confirmed that its core AI model weights, source code, and customer chatbot conversations remained secure during the incident.
- The company disabled the affected software immediately after its monitoring systems flagged the unauthorized activity.
- Anthropic reported the incident to federal officials, though it disputes Cathedral's claims regarding the severity of the national security implications.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing risks associated with AI agents navigating third-party business software and the potential for automated tools to bypass standard security protocols. It underscores the urgent need for companies to strengthen supply chain security as AI-driven cyber threats become increasingly sophisticated and difficult to manage.

results.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
results.author: Paresh Dave
results.content:
Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.
Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.
Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”
While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”
The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.
Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.
Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.
Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.
Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents.
Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said.
Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email.
There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement.
Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent. But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.
results.summary:
Meta’s agentic AI tool, Muse, is seeing limited commercial adoption despite high user engagement, prompting major corporations to begin optimizing their websites for future automated shopping integration.

### Key Points
- Meta reports over 10 million users for Muse in the U.S. and Canada, with more than 25 percent utilizing the tool for shopping tasks.
- Major companies including DoorDash, Hilton, and Ally Financial report that current transaction volumes originating from AI agents remain insignificant.
- Chipotle and other retailers are actively updating website code to resolve technical issues that prevent AI agents from successfully completing customer orders.
- Meta plans to eventually monetize Muse by charging businesses transaction fees, potentially creating a revenue stream that could surpass its advertising business.
- Bank of America and other financial institutions have issued security warnings regarding the risks of sharing user credentials with third-party AI assistants.
- Amazon and Insurify have shifted their strategies, moving from blocking Muse to exploring ways to integrate or collaborate with external AI shopping agents.

### Why it Matters
While current transaction volumes remain low, businesses are proactively adjusting their digital infrastructure to prepare for a potential shift toward AI-driven commerce. This transition highlights a growing tension between the convenience of automated shopping and the need for companies to maintain brand loyalty, data security, and profit margins.

results.title: XBOX made generational leaps with each console — So, what happens next?
results.author: ben.wilson@windowscentral.com (Ben Wilson) , Ben Wilson
results.content:
The official XBOX 25th anniversary is approaching fast, with November 15 flanked on both sides by plans for special hardware, celebratory merchandise, and a wave of themed cosmetics from Microsoft's gaming division.
It's almost hard to comprehend, given that I remember the much-anticipated launch of the original XBOX quite clearly.
But time marches on, and XBOX has proven it can iterate its hardware and innovate its experiences over the years.
So, in another mix of self-indulgent nostalgia and reflection on how far the technology has come, I'm looking back at how far performance has leaped across these console generations, from the original XBOX to the Series X and beyond.
XBOX (2001)
Microsoft's first console was comically gigantic and heavy, packed with parts that felt at home in a mid-to-high-tier desktop PC of the time. Its DVD drive sat alongside a 3.5-inch hard drive with 8–10 GB of space, connected via old-school IDE ribbon cables, and together they made up most of the heft. Some of my braver friends replaced their HDDs, requiring injected softmods to work.
Deeper inside, Intel provided a modified Pentium III x86 CPU built on a 180 nm process, which it has since scaled down incredibly far to the latest 18A process node used in its mainstream chips. Running at 733 MHz, the processor sat alongside 64 MB of DDR RAM (that's megabytes, not gigabytes) clocked at 200 MHz and an NVIDIA GeForce 3-based GPU at 233 MHz.
Looking back, it's fascinating how the OG XBOX resembled many of my friends' PCs at the time; we either paired Intel CPUs with NVIDIA GPUs or opted for AMD CPUs with ATI (later acquired by AMD) GPUs. It wasn't a permanent partnership for Microsoft, but it powered a compelling competitor to Sony's PlayStation 2, even if it remained out of reach for my teenage self.
XBOX 360 (2005)
Design-wise, this slim console was a far cry from its behemoth predecessor. Sure enough, the XBOX 360 made an instant impression on me and an even faster dent in my first self-earned paychecks. This time, Microsoft opted for a 64-bit PowerPC-based CPU design from IBM, moving further away from traditional PC architecture, with a massive clock speed jump to 3.2 GHz in its tri-core chip.
This leap to a multi-core processor makes direct clock speed comparisons a little moot, but it's still impressive to see how far the XBOX jumped in one generation. Its unified memory moved from DDR SDRAM to 512 MB of GDDR3 RAM clocked at 700 MHz for eight times more capacity and triple the bandwidth, and the GPU swapped teams to the ATI-designed 'Xenos' at 500 MHz.
Storage space is where it gets harder to define, because Microsoft offered so many different models, redesigns, and expandable add-ons. The earliest XBOX 360 consoles I saw ranged from selling with no hard drive at all to a 'Premium' model with a 20 GB HDD in the box. For game discs, Microsoft kept DVDs, but increased the read speed and moved to a SATA-connected, dual-layer disc drive.
XBOX One (2013)
Ah, the all-in-one entertainment unit. I bought into the XBOX ONE so eagerly because I wanted to play Quantum Break, but I was also intrigued by its appeal as a TV tuner with live programming snapped to the side of my screen. Of course, I'd never get the promised DVR function, and the Kinect 2.0 sensor did little more than collect dust, but the console still had its gaming appeal.
This is when Microsoft's consoles started resembling PCs again, with an octo-core AMD Jaguar CPU running x86-64 instructions, clocked at 1.75 GHz. It wasn't as mind-blowing as the XBOX 360's evolution, but the XBOX ONE came with 8GB of DDR3 RAM for a 16x generational memory capacity leap; all part of a new console that was generally easier for game developers to target.
This is also where Microsoft's modern AMD era began, building a GPU running at 853 MHz into its singular APU and delivering raw graphical compute performance about five times faster than the XBOX 360. Storage saw a huge jump to 500 GB to support game installations, and Microsoft finally adopted Blu-ray with a BD-ROM disc drive, but games were already going digital.
XBOX Series X (2020)
Yes, the current generation is almost six years old. We're once again entering an age of speculation about what comes next, but the XBOX Series X (and Series S) remain the brand's primary focus. There's even a transparent green 'Xbox Series X25' special edition console and controller launching in November, though I'm still quite satisfied with my original Series X|S variants.
The specs have more nuance these days, but the AMD octo-core Zen 2 CPU runs at 3.66 GHz, paired with an AMD RDNA 2 GPU at 1.82 GHz in another custom APU. For unified memory, Microsoft moved up to 16 GB of GDDR6 RAM, while storage starts with a 1 TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, depending on the model you choose. Proprietary external storage also returned this generation, up to 4 TB.
An Ultra HD Blu-ray drive was also standard at launch, but later 'All-Digital' models have dropped it, in keeping with an ongoing trend shift towards digital gaming. Some major releases are already launching without physical media, and it's reasonable to assume that the Series X could be Microsoft's last console to support them by default.
XBOX Project Helix (2028?)
So, what comes next? We already know that Project Helix will be "powered by a custom AMD SoC", much like the APUs in previous XBOX consoles, and that high-end visuals are a focus for the brand. Ray-tracing technology, in particular, delivers incredibly realistic lighting, reflections, and shadows, but it's demanding on any hardware, which is where AI comes in.
AMD's FidelityFX Super Resolution (FSR) upscaling tech is already making its way to current-gen XBOX consoles via FSR 4.1, and early testing with beta drivers on XBOX Ally handheld gaming PCs shows some promise for improved visual fidelity at the same performance. A new AI-assisted upscaler seems likely for the next XBOX, but it'll depend on what AMD can support with its hardware plans.
Of course, the utterly gigantic elephant in the room right now is the ongoing memory crisis. Shortages have pushed up the cost of components and completely removed some of the highest-end consumer GPUs from sale, as major brands like NVIDIA focus on hardware for large-scale artificial intelligence platforms instead. It'll likely be the most PC-like console yet, but at a severe cost.
Its literal cost will continue to be the most pressing prediction posed by long-serving XBOX gamers. Both of the Series X|S consoles already suffered a price hike, which has many wondering what they'll have to pay for the next-generation console. Is $1,000+ a realistic expectation, or can Microsoft pull some favors to offset the inflated manufacturing costs? Let's see what 2027 reveals.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Ben is a Senior Editor of Windows Central, covering PC gaming hardware, software, and everything connected to it. He's built more custom desktops than he can count, and has hands-on experience with some of the most exciting components and accessories for Windows PC and Xbox. A lifelong obsession with Microsoft's technology has led to broad expertise in laptops and in the cutting-edge processors that are pushing the industry forward.

results.title: Kushner book author reveals bombshell detail he left out about hacked phone
results.author: Bennito L. Kelty
results.content:
The author of a bombshell book on Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner's alleged Gulf dealings just revealed something about a hacked phone his book left out.
Investigative journalist Matthew Cole, whose new book "Princes and Thieves" alleges Kushner had access to secret Gulf-funded bank accounts while serving in the White House, told host Molly Jong-Fast on Saturday's episode of "Fast Politics" that his reporting points to other U.S. allies knowing about Dutch intelligence services hacking Kushner's phone.
"There are some indications in my reporting, which are not in the book because it gets complicated, that there are other European, other NATO allies that have seen or are aware that the Dutch were in there and that they had access to Kushner's phone," Cole told Jong-Fast.
As Gizmodo reported, Cole's book alleges that Dutch military intelligence found screenshots from Kushner's iPhone on a Russian military intelligence server and later exploited the same weakness to watch his screen, catching him logging into a Dubai-based account that had taken in hundreds of millions of dollars.
Cole described that access as limited.
"It wasn't malware where they could manipulate the phone, but they had the ability to see the phone when the phone was on," he noted.
Cole also took on a question that "Daily Show" host Jon Stewart pressed him on earlier this week, namely why the Dutch never alerted Washington.
"The U.S. is a NATO ally. Intelligence agencies keep secrets. That is literally what they do for a living," Cole told Jong-Fast. "If they can get into something, they will. And if they can gather something, they will."
He added that he had "no indication at all" that the Dutch shared what they found with the U.S. government, though he allowed it was possible.
Cole framed the episode as a sign of how little the public knows about what happens behind closed doors.
"At least in foreign policy, our government has shrunk to like three people, essentially a family and a few friends," he said.
Asked whether his reporting captured only a sliver of a larger story, Cole said his work was extensive but much of what lies beneath it remains hidden.
"What my reporting shows is this is the tip of the iceberg," Cole explained. "I don't know how big the iceberg is, and I don't pretend to."
Cole noted that Kushner and his lawyer "unequivocally and emphatically deny every allegation in the book." Kushner has publicly dismissed the claims.
results.summary:
Investigative journalist Matthew Cole reports that Dutch intelligence allegedly hacked Jared Kushner’s phone, revealing potential access to secret Gulf-funded bank accounts during his tenure in the White House.

### Key Points
- Investigative journalist Matthew Cole alleges in his book "Princes and Thieves" that Dutch military intelligence accessed Jared Kushner’s iPhone.
- The report claims Dutch intelligence discovered screenshots of Kushner’s phone on a Russian server and subsequently monitored his activity.
- Cole states that other NATO allies were reportedly aware of the Dutch intelligence operation involving Kushner’s device.
- The book alleges Kushner accessed a Dubai-based account containing hundreds of millions of dollars while serving as a senior White House official.
- Jared Kushner and his legal representatives have issued an emphatic denial regarding all allegations presented in the book.

### Why it Matters
These allegations raise significant questions regarding national security protocols and the potential vulnerability of high-ranking U.S. officials to foreign intelligence surveillance. If verified, the report suggests a major breach of diplomatic trust between the United States and its NATO allies.

results.title: Monthly News – October 2026
results.author: Clem
results.content:
Hello everyone,
Before we start with the news, I’d like to thank all the people who support this project. Your help is greatly appreciated. Thank you.
As always, please note that the features presented below are a preview. They’re still being worked on and are planned for the next version of Linux Mint.
Sleep Modes
When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful. It’s well supported, fast and reliable, but it has a major limitation: It uses power.
A good laptop with a full battery can sleep for 2 or 3 days, but eventually the battery runs out. When it does, the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.
Unfortunately, this happens often because the typical use case for Suspend is that you’re done using the laptop and you want to go and do something else. Closing the lid is fast. Looking for the power cable isn’t. And the computer looks like it’s OFF, so you might not even think about it.
This is where “Hibernation” comes into play. Hibernation saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was and so is the battery.
Unlike Suspend, though, Hibernation is slow. It can take longer than a reboot to hibernate and resume the computer.
Hibernation is also hard to set up. It doesn’t work out of the box and requires a large amount of swap space on disk. Ubuntu actually decided to remove it from the available sleep modes, so it was usually not available in Linux Mint.
We’re bringing it back.
We added a page in the System Administration tool dedicated to Sleep Modes.
This page makes it easy to enable Hibernation and to set it up correctly.
We also took the opportunity to add support for Hybrid Sleep and Suspend-then-Hibernate.
Hybrid Sleep suspends the computer but also saves the session to disk. If the battery runs out, you need to find the power cable, but you can resume the session.
As the name suggests, Suspend-then-Hibernate suspends the computer but when the battery level goes critical, it hibernates it.
Nemo Preview Pane
The file manager got a preview pane.
You can toggle it with F7 or by clicking the button in the status bar.
The preview pane supports audio, pictures and videos.
It also shows information about the selected media. For instance, in the screenshot above you can see when the picture was taken, and with which camera.
Superlight
Superlight is a new application whose purpose is to monitor the state of the system.
It shows graphs for CPU and RAM usage, but also SWAP, GPU, Network, Disk I/O, Temperature and Fan Speed.
On its App page, you can see what’s running on the computer and how much of the system’s resources each application is using.
You can also see the same data for all the running processes.
You can choose from a large variety of columns, and sort them or reorder them any way you like. All of this is remembered by Superlight.
If you have a battery, you can see its status, all the information related to it, and a history of charge level and power input/output.
The Storage page shows how much space is used on your disks and what’s using it.
You start with a general breakdown. If you click on Files, you can browse and see which folders and files take up the most space.
If you click on Steam, Superlight shows you which games take up space.
And the same goes for Flatpak.
Superlight makes it easy to see what’s taking up resources on your computer.
Velocitty
Velocitty is a new terminal application. It’s really simple to use and packed with great features.
Like Ghostty and Ptyxis, it comes with a tab overview:
And it can be themed with palettes:
Just like in Firefox, you can reorder tabs within a window, move them from one terminal window to another, or even detach a tab into a new window.
You can choose which shell to run and specify a startup command. Here’s Velocitty configured to use fish and run fastfetch at startup:
Paths can be shortened in the preferences. For instance, here’s /var/lib/dpkg/info shortened to just info in the tab name and …/lib/dpkg/info in the prompt.
The color of the tab changes when something is going on. Red for superuser (root, sudo, pkexec, etc.), blue for remote sessions (ssh, sftp, etc.), and a lighter shade for running processes.
And tabs can be customized. You can give them a name, a color, a command to run and decide if you want them to automatically open when you launch Velocitty.
Clicking the little bookmark icon opens up all your custom tabs.
So whatever you’re working on, your projects and SSH sessions are always really easy to access.
Unfold
Unfold is a small archive manager designed to be as simple and easy to use as possible.
It supports basic operations such as viewing, creating and extracting archives.
It uses 7zip and 7zip-RAR and it’s compatible with all the encryption formats they support, including password-protected ones.
Other News
Xenity is a fork of Zenity 3.44 (GTK3), with the same features, the same look and the same syntax. It was added to the Mint 22.x and LMDE 7 repositories, and all Cinnamon spices which used Zenity were migrated to Xenity.
The Community Website was written years ago. It used PHP and allowed people to create accounts with a login and password. Following the recent discovery of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, we decided to rewrite it from scratch and reduce the amount of sensitive data stored in our database. It no longer uses PHP and it no longer stores or uses passwords. Authentication is now handled by GitHub. When you sign in, the Community Website gets the following data from GitHub: your username, your email address, and your avatar. If your email address matches the email associated with an existing account, that account is merged into the new one.

results.title: ASML’s CEO is putting his paycheck on the line for employee morale. It could help retain talent that’s nearly impossible to replace
results.author: Muskaan Arshad
results.content:
ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet is putting his own paycheck on the line for employee morale.
In a memo to staff first reported by Business Insider, Fouquet said the Dutch chip-equipment maker will build a new Workplace Experience Index into the long-term incentive plan for its senior leaders, including himself and the rest of ASML’s Board of Management. “In the coming years, it will directly influence the remuneration of senior leaders, including the Board of Management,” Fouquet wrote.
The change follows ASML’s annual employee survey, which found the company’s engagement index fell to 73.5% this year from 78% in 2025. More than 38,000 of ASML’s roughly 44,000 employees took part. Fouquet acknowledged the drop came after a “disruptive and emotional year” for the company.
The new index is built from six survey questions, ranging from whether employees trust senior leadership to make the right decisions to whether they feel safe speaking up, understand their roles, believe their teams operate effectively, and feel their direct manager cares about them. The memo doesn’t say how much weight the index will carry in executive pay or when it will first be applied.
Tying top executives’ compensation to employee sentiment is uncommon but not unprecedented; IBM and Aviva have previously included engagement in their executive pay targets, Business Insider noted.
A tumultuous year at a company the AI boom depends on
ASML is the world’s only supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which are essential for producing the most advanced semiconductors. The company has benefited enormously from the hundreds of billions of dollars tech giants are pouring into AI infrastructure, posting a record net profit of €9.6 billion in 2025.
Even so, on the same day it reported those results in January, ASML announced plans to cut about 1,700 positions, roughly 3.8% of its workforce, mostly in management roles within its technology and IT organizations in the Netherlands and the U.S. The goal, the company said, was to strip out bureaucracy and free its engineers to focus on innovation.
Dutch unions pushed back hard. The CNV union said it was “completely taken aback” by the plan, NL Times reported. ASML ultimately negotiated a social plan with four unions (FNV, CNV, De Unie, and VHP2), agreed in principle in May and finalized in June. The deal bars compulsory layoffs until May 1, 2027, and leans on internal redeployment that the company said could save several hundred jobs.
In his memo, Fouquet tied the slide in engagement to that upheaval, citing the restructuring turmoil as the reason for linking leadership pay to how employees experience the company.
Why is ASML tying executive pay to employee satisfaction?
Much of the tech world has moved in the opposite direction, embracing long hours and repeated rounds of layoffs. Some startups have even adopted the “996” schedule, a practice borrowed from China’s tech industry that requires employees to work from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.
Job cuts have piled up, too. U.S. employers announced about 1.2 million job cuts in 2025, the most since 2020 and roughly on par with 2008, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. Technology led the private sector with 154,445 announced cuts. Overall announced cuts have eased in 2026, falling 39% to 573,195 through September, but tech is moving the other way: the sector’s 165,925 cuts so far this year are up 54% and account for 29% of all job cuts, Challenger’s September report found.
The cuts have continued this month. Netflix said it would lay off roughly 1,000 employees, about 6% of its workforce. Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff. And Skydance, the company formed by Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, warned employees that layoffs are coming.
But ASML faces a different calculus, says Martijn Hendriks, deputy scientific director of the Erasmus Happiness Economics Research Organization, who has studied employee engagement and CEO compensation. Because its workforce is so specialized, he argues, ASML has more reason than most tech giants to prioritize employee satisfaction.
“The reason ASML does this is because for them attracting talent and keeping talent is like crucial,” Hendriks tells Fortune. “They invest a lot in well-being because these people are so specialized that replacing them just costs a lot of money.”
Does CEO compensation affect employees?
ASML is tying executive pay to employee satisfaction at a moment when soaring CEO compensation is fueling questions about fairness.
The 1,500 top-paid CEOs worldwide received an average 11% real-terms raise in 2025, while the average worker saw just 0.5%, according to a study by the International Trade Union Confederation and Oxfam. Those CEOs earned an average of $8.4 million last year, up from an inflation-adjusted $5.5 million in 2019, Fortune reported.
Elon Musk has been at the center of the debate. He became the world’s first trillionaire in June after SpaceX’s record IPO, and his fortune has hovered around that mark since. Tesla shareholders approved a pay package in November 2025 that could award him up to $1 trillion in stock if he hits a series of performance targets. The AFL-CIO valued Musk’s 2025 Tesla compensation at $158.3 billion, about 2.5 million times what Tesla’s median employee earned: $57,243.
Hendriks says that, in general, there isn’t a direct link between employee engagement and CEO compensation. But engagement can decline sharply when media coverage spotlights extreme pay packages like Musk’s, he says.
Those situations can seriously affect employee performance, according to Trevor Watkins, a University of Oklahoma professor who studies organizational behavior.
When fairness is absent, Watkins tells Fortune, “the predicted outcome is going to be anger and resentment.”
“These emotions do not bode well for what organizations care about with respect to their workforce. They want them to be engaged and productive, and these perceptions of unfairness and resentment interfere with that.”
results.summary:
ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet will link executive compensation to a new internal Workplace Experience Index following a significant decline in employee engagement scores across the semiconductor company.

### Key Points
- ASML’s employee engagement index dropped from 78% in 2025 to 73.5% this year.
- The new index measures six factors, including leadership trust, psychological safety, and team effectiveness.
- This policy change applies to the Board of Management and senior leadership to address morale after recent restructuring.
- ASML previously announced plans to cut 1,700 positions, leading to negotiations with four Dutch labor unions.
- The company relies on highly specialized talent, making the retention of its 44,000 employees critical to maintaining its EUV lithography market dominance.

### Why it Matters
Linking executive pay to staff sentiment serves as a strategic effort to stabilize a workforce essential for producing the world's most advanced AI-enabling hardware. By prioritizing internal culture, ASML aims to mitigate the risks of turnover and resentment that often follow large-scale corporate restructuring.

results.title: The AI sell-off is exposing the risks of betting on Wall Street’s favorite stocks
results.author: Jared Blikre
results.content:
Wall Street analysts spent 2026 piling Buy ratings onto the AI build-out. The stocks they ignored have done better.
The S&P 500 (^GSPC) stocks with the biggest share of analyst Buy ratings have trailed those with the smallest share for most of the year, according to Piper Sandler chief investment strategist Michael Kantrowitz. Measured year over year, it's the third-worst stretch in Piper's data going back to 1995.
"The Sell Side's MOST favored stocks have underperformed their LEAST favored stocks for the majority of 2026," Kantrowitz wrote in a note to clients Wednesday.
This week showed what that looks like. Alphabet had its worst month in history, Intel had its worst day since 1974, and the Nasdaq (^IXIC) suffered its biggest daily drop since June as Big Tech's results revived worries about AI spending.
Add it up, and the AI trade has lost about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations, including about $1.6 trillion on Friday alone. Nvidia and Alphabet, two of Piper's favorites, shed about $835 billion each, roughly a third of the total.
The rest of the market has held up. The other 625 large US stocks in Yahoo Finance's count gained about $1.3 trillion over the same stretch, led by Eli Lilly (LLY), Walmart (WMT) and Exxon Mobil (XOM). It's the slump in Wall Street's favorites, playing out in a single month.
Piper picks both groups from the top and bottom of each of the index's 11 sectors, so this isn't tech against everything else.
Only two slumps ran deeper, in 2001-02 and 2010. Both came near big turning points in the market, the first as the tech bubble deflated and the second as stocks recovered from the financial crisis.
Why this hits more portfolios than you'd think
Most investors own Wall Street's favorites whether they picked them or not. Nvidia (NVDA) and Alphabet (GOOGL) are among the biggest weights in the S&P 500, so any index fund or 401(k) that tracks it leans on their fortunes.
The slump also shows how a crowded idea can work against investors. When nearly every analyst already loves a stock, much of the good news is in the price, and there are few new buyers left to win over. A disappointment then stings.
That's what the favorites are running into. Six of the nine names on Piper's list are down this year, from Alphabet and power producer Vistra (VST) to Wynn Resorts (WYNN) and Take-Two Interactive (TTWO). The exceptions are three AI build-out names: Nvidia, Arista Networks (ANET), and Comfort Systems (FIX).
Meanwhile, nearly all of the least-loved stocks are up, led by steady names like Kenvue (KVUE) and Illinois Tool Works (ITW). As a group, though, they've only roughly kept pace with the S&P 500. This is less about the laggards running than about the favorites falling.
results.summary:
S&P 500 stocks with the highest concentration of analyst Buy ratings have significantly underperformed less-favored equities throughout 2026, marking the third-worst performance stretch since 1995.

### Key Points
- Piper Sandler strategist Michael Kantrowitz reports that Wall Street’s most favored stocks are currently trailing the least-favored group.
- The AI-focused trade has lost approximately $5 trillion in market value since October 6, with Nvidia and Alphabet accounting for significant portions of that decline.
- Large-cap stocks like Eli Lilly, Walmart, and Exxon Mobil have gained $1.3 trillion during the same period, providing a buffer against the tech-heavy slump.
- Six of the nine stocks on Piper Sandler’s "most favored" list have declined in value throughout 2026.
- Historical data shows similar underperformance patterns occurred only in 2001-02 and 2010, both of which preceded major market turning points.

### Why it Matters
The underperformance of analyst-favored stocks highlights the risks of crowded trades where positive expectations are already fully priced into valuations. Because these companies hold significant weight in major indices, their volatility directly impacts the performance of most retail 401(k) plans and passive index funds.

results.title: Flying cars are coming. You’ll need $300K and the space to fly it.
results.author: Lloyd Lee
results.content:
Flying cars could be around the corner. Just don't expect them to be part of your daily commute anytime soon.
Two days before Tesla's demonstration of its kickflipping Roadster put flying cars back in the spotlight, a startup that has been building flying cars since 2015 posted a video-slash-salvo of a test model hovering over a Tesla Cybertruck and an early-generation Roadster.
"A lot of people now are aware of the Roadster, but we were already flying for five years," Jim Dukhovny, CEO of Alef Aeronautics, told Business Insider, adding that they have logged about 1,000 flights. 
Alef planned the video response about a month before the Roadster demo, after reports indicated Tesla might debut a flying car, he said.
As for when flying cars will actually be delivered to the public, Tesla said its Roadster will start production in 2028, but the version that includes a "full flight system" will be invite-only. Meanwhile, Dukhovny said his company hopes to deliver its first car by next year.
There are hefty price tags for both: Alef Aeronautics expects its flying car to cost $300,000 with a $150 preorder deposit. Tesla doesn't display the full price of the Roadster. The company website states the Roadster with "acceleration thrusters" requires a $250,000 deposit.
Dukhovny said the cost for a flying car is too high — even for him.
"I cannot afford it right now," he said about purchasing one, adding, "Once we go to mass production and once we get to the scale of automotive manufacturing, that should cost under $25,000."
Price isn't the only barrier. You'll also need a place to fly it.
Dukhovny, who is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, said that while we may not need dedicated heliports for flying cars, we shouldn't expect to take off somewhere in the middle of downtown to avoid traffic.
"You cannot take off from Market Street or land on Market Street," he said, referring to a major San Francisco artery. "Not right now, not ever. You have to take off and land from places where it's allowed, but you don't have to build that."
Alexandre Bayen, an electrical engineering and computer science professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies advanced transportation systems, said the technology behind flying cars isn't the challenge; rather, it's building a reliable transit system with those cars.
Factoring in regulations, infrastructure, and public acceptance, Bayen said a world in which people in dense urban areas can travel by flying car is likely generations away.
"Thinking of this as a vehicle for mass transit in the near future is, I think, absolutely unrealistic," he said.
Dukhonvy said he imagines early use cases revolving around people living in remote locations — think mountainous terrain or areas with underdeveloped roads. The CEO framed it as a cost- and time-saving measure for the wealthy.
Bayen similarly said he could see flying-car technology being useful for short commutes over small bodies of water.
"The one type of demand that this type of technology solves is a very elite shortcut commute above water or obstacles for people who can afford it," he said.
Companies like Joby Aircraft and Archer Aviation are building an air transit system with eVTOLs — electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft — that are similar to helicopters but quieter and powered by electricity.
Dukhovny stressed that flying cars are different because they can drive on roads.
"Right now, there are only two that exist," he said. "Us and Tesla."
A Tesla spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
results.summary:
Alef Aeronautics and Tesla are advancing flying car technology, though experts warn that regulatory hurdles and infrastructure limitations make widespread urban adoption unlikely for the foreseeable future.

### Key Points
- Alef Aeronautics aims to deliver its first flying car by 2025, with a projected retail price of $300,000.
- Tesla plans to begin production of its Roadster, featuring an optional "full flight system," in 2028.
- Alef Aeronautics has logged approximately 1,000 test flights since 2015, according to CEO Jim Dukhovny.
- Experts like UC Berkeley professor Alexandre Bayen argue that mass transit via flying cars remains generations away due to regulatory and infrastructure challenges.
- Current industry focus is shifting toward elite, short-distance travel over water or obstacles rather than daily urban commuting.

### Why it Matters
The development of flying cars highlights a growing divide between high-end technological innovation and the practical realities of modern transportation infrastructure. While these vehicles may offer niche solutions for remote travel, significant regulatory and safety barriers suggest they will remain luxury items rather than viable mass-transit alternatives for the general public.

results.title: You only need one fast charger for your iPhone, Samsung, and Pixel, but it needs this feature
results.author: Brady Snyder
results.content:
I've completely switched over to USB-C gadgets, and that means the same charger can power everything from my camera and smartphones to my over-ear headphones and laptops. It's the universal charging experience I always wanted, with a caveat. Each device has unique requirements that must be met by a USB-C cable and power adapter in order to charge at their fastest speeds. Apple, Samsung, and Google all tout fast wired charging speeds, but you won't see them using any old charger.
Although the USB Power Delivery standard was supposed to simplify matters, it hasn't. It's no longer enough to check for the USB PD certification on the box of a new charger. You need a USB PD power adapter with Programmable Power Supply (PPS) support, and it must be 27W or higher. Find a charger that checks all those boxes, and you'll be able to charge any iPhone, Pixel, or Galaxy at their top speeds.
Pixel and Galaxy phones need PPS
This feature lets your phone charge at its fastest
The latest phones from Samsung and Google don't charge as fast as their global competitors, but to achieve their peak charging performance, you need a PPS charger. The Google Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold all charge at 30W over a cable. The high-end Pixel 11 Pro XL charges at a faster 45W rate. Meanwhile, the Galaxy S26, Galaxy S26 Plus, and Galaxy S26 Ultra charge at 25W, 45W, and 60W wired speeds, respectively.
Those advertised speeds are only attainable with a certified USB PD charger with PPS support. Older chargers could only adjust real-time wattage and voltage within pre-set tiers. Your smartphone negotiates how much power is delivered based on how much it can accept. This changes dynamically based on the phone's battery level and temperature. However, if a charger can't match the exact voltage a phone is asking for, it has to step down to a lower pre-set tier.
This results in slower charging speeds, and it's why PPS is important. PPS chargers can adjust their voltage more fluidly, between 3.3V and 21V. The voltage and current are tweaked in small, precise increments. Specifically, a PPS charger is capable of adjusting voltage and current in 20mV and 50mA steps.
Pixel and Galaxy phones leverage PPS chargers to avoid leaving faster charging speeds on the table. An old-school USB PD charger could be limited to imprecise 15V and 9V steps — a phone that wants to accept a voltage somewhere in the middle must step all the way down to 9V and charge slower. With a PPS charger, a Pixel or Galaxy phone can charge at the exact voltage and current tier it requests, within 20mV and 50mA increments.
After you've found a PPS charger for your devices, you'll want to check its wattage and maximum voltage capabilities.
Not any PPS charger will do the job
iPhones are picky, and need a PPS charger with AVS
I wish it were as simple as picking up a USB PD charger with PPS support, but it's not. You'll need to first make sure the PPS charger you're considering supports a wide enough voltage range. While some power adapters with PPS compatibility are limited to 11V or 16V maximums, some phones require PPS chargers to reach 21V. The Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro only need 11V PPS chargers, but the Pixel 11 Pro XL requires a 21V PPS charger.
iPhones require a fast-charging standard of their own called Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS). It's quite similar to PPS, but AVS is more limited in its voltage range and the scope of its adjustments. Chargers with AVS can fluctuate between 9V and 20V, and the adjustments come in 100mV increments. It's not as versatile as PPS, which can move between 3.3V and 21V in 20mV increments.
AVS is a lesser version of PPS, and the good news is that the best PPS chargers support both standards. Any charger that meets the USB PD 3.2 specification, supports PPS, and can deliver at least 27W of power also has AVS support. It works within the USB PD standard power range, which covers chargers between 27W and 100W.
Grab a charger with USB PD 3.2 PPS support, between 27W and 100W, and you'll be able to charge any iPhone, Pixel, or Galaxy.
One charger to rule them all
This charger can power my laptops, too
Charging specifications clearly still need work, because finding the right power adapter for all your devices entails completing a three-part checklist. Google has a charger with USB PD 3.2, PPS, and AVS support — the Pixel Flex Dual 67W charger — and it's the most versatile power adapter I've tested. It can charge just about any USB-C device at its peak speeds, save for power-hungry laptops.
However, Google is far from the only company making fast USB PD chargers. Any certified USB PD 3.2 charger between 27W and 100W with PPS will do the trick, so you can pick the one you like best.

results.title: The Samsung News app is being discontinued, and there's no replacement yet
results.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
results.content:
Samsung is about to kill another built-in Galaxy feature, and this time it's the news feed that many users probably haven't noticed anymore.
In a confirmation from the company spotted by SamMobile, the Samsung News app will be discontinued on December 21, 2026, at 00:00 UTC — leaving Galaxy phone and tablet owners bereft of one of the platform’s familiar ways to catch up on daily headlines.
The shutdown will affect more than just the Samsung News app. Its home screen widget will no longer get updated with new content, and the media page you can access by swiping right from the leftmost home screen will be gone.
Samsung has already begun sending shutdown notices to users in India and South Korea, urging them to remove the widget before the service is discontinued.
Samsung will also erase all user data related to the service after the shutdown. This includes personal information, account profiles, and personalization settings. Some information may be kept temporarily, as mandated by local law, but Samsung says it will be deleted eventually.
Samsung News is not new. It launched in April 2023, succeeding Samsung Free, and continuing a surprisingly long line of shuttered news-feed services. Samsung Free replaced Samsung Daily in 2020 and Bixby Home replaced Samsung Daily in 2019. That's quite a few rebrands for something that ultimately ended up on the chopping block.
So, what comes next? Samsung hasn’t announced a direct replacement, but Google Discover is a likely candidate. The service is already available as an alternative on Galaxy devices, so this is a convenient option if Samsung chooses to simplify its software experience.

While these confirmed shutdown notices are for India and South Korea, owners in other markets should be watching for similar announcements, rather than assuming their regional service will disappear on the same schedule. In any case, it seems Samsung’s native news experience is headed for its final headline.
