results.title: October 2026 in Review
results.author: Wilhelm Arcturus
results.content:
The Site
WordPress.com announced this past month that paid plans will be allowed to upload premium themes downloaded or purchased outside of the stock selection they maintain. Or fail to maintain, which is probably the real reason for this.
I have suddenly gone from “All the supported themes kind of suck for my needs” to “There are too many choices!” So I’ll have to see if I can wrestle with that problem.
Also in this month was the PHP2Shell critical vulnerabilities crisis that got a lot of site owners in a panic. WP.com assured us that sites it hosted were all protected… and what would I be able to do about it in any case?
Then there was the Monday morning I woke up and found that the classic editor had once again disappeared from the hosting panel. The block editor is probably fine for something, but writing isn’t it. This turned out to be related to a changed WP.com made to the dashboard settings, where if you are set to “default” you get the classic editor and if you are set to “classic” you do NOT get the classic editor. Somebody make sense of that.
Anyway, I was back up and running by lunch.
And then, somewhere along the line in October, the site passed the 8,000 post mark. I didn’t know you could stack crap that high, but here we are.
One Year Ago
The deal for the Saudis and Jared Kushner to buy out Electronic Arts had been finalized and approved and I was saying farewell to whatever the company meant at that point.
Amazon Games gave up on big online games, announcing New World would be closing and that their ever changing plans for something in Middle-earth would be changing again. They were more interested in AI driven slop like their Snoop Dogg voiced Chaos in Court title.
There was also the big Pokemon Go update that boosted the level cap to 80… which was a bit of a let down actually.
Over on the Enad Global 7 front I was wondering if we were going to get any EverQuest 3 news.
With that not forthcoming, EverQuest did announce the Shattering of Ro expansion, while EverQuest II did the same for the Rage of Cthurath expansion.
Meanwhile, on the LOTRO front, SSG was giving people a chance to transfer characters off of the recently closed 32-bit worlds.
I was also wondering if we were going to see any more updates in No Man’s Sky to follow up Voyagers and expand on the corvette thing. They seemed to lack for a landing pad, for starters. The Breach expedition did give us some new corvette parts at least. I went off to try that. Potshot and I also started to search for a paradise planet to settle on.
Over in New Eden CCP launched the annual Crimson Harvest event. They also announced the candidate list for the CSM20 election, published the September 2025 economic report, announced the upcoming Catalyst expansion, kicked off Alliance Tournament XXI, began the CSM20 elections, and ramped up the final week of Crimson Harvest with new rewards.
In null sec Fraternity announced its invasion of The Initiative space, something they would never, ever come to regret, and PanFam pulled back their staging system, a portent to their coming collapse.
Also, the Reavers SIG turned eleven, though it existed mostly as a Discord chat channel by then.
In Palworld we were poaching in the No.1 Wildlife Sanctuary after which we were off to the mountain cold. The it was on to a fiery mountainside climb.
We were also taking a look at the cozy title Palia. We ran around and made ramen together.
In a Friday bullet points post I looked into Valheim coming to PlayStation, Microsoft laying people off and raising the price of XBox game pass, Sackbird studios being formed from layoff refugees, the demise of Greg Street’s Fantastic Pixel Castle plans, Embracer spinning off Coffee Stain while loading it with debt, and Ship of Heroes complaining about being review bombed.
And on the streaming front we watched Kaos with Jeff Goldblum, Rick & Morty season 8, and House of Guinness. I wrote whole posts about each.
Five Years Ago
In a bit of irony I unleashed ads on the site in order to pay for the premium WordPress.com plan, otherwise they would be unleashing ads on the site. But at least I was getting some of that ad money guess. I kept that up every so often before finally deciding I had done that enough.
Facebook changes its name to Meta and Mark Zuckerberg announced they were going all-in on the idea of a VR based online metaverse. John Carmack had some issues with the plan, while reality… made Zuck look like the man-boy dumbshit he is. Nothing since has changed my view on that.
Then acting EG7 CEO Ji Ham spoke about the company and its plans. Meanwhile EverQuest announced the Terror of Luclin expansion and EverQuest II announced the Visions of Vertovia expansion. It was also Panda time in EQII.
Those expansions got me on to a bit of a comparison between the EQ expansion machine and WoW.
Blizzard announced the WoW Classic Season of Mastery plan, set to launch in November, an attempt to give a slightly different vanilla experience… and a temporary one at that as it closed down just a year later.
There would also be no BlizzCon 2022. Covid and stuff.
We were getting into Diablo II Resurrected as a group. We remade our group after a bit, working our way through the first act. We got stuck into Act II pretty quickly, making it through to the end.
On my own I played a necromancer through the first difficultly level. I was playing on Battle.net for some reason, where there were queues to get online.
Carbot and Honest Game Trailers had their own special D2R videos.
Amazon Games’ New World was live and I was trying to play… though there were issues.
In EVE Online there was a bit of a mining boom in the wake of World War Bee. CCP was also going back to native MacOS support. They also introduced CRAB beacons to the game and changed the tax structure. And then there was the return of the Crimson Harvest event.
the Reavers SIG turned seven years old.
I also did an EVE Online Friday Bullet Points post about Quasar, Totality Day, Faction Warfare, mega skill point offers, monocles, and an exploration of the new user experience.
In my series on immersion I tackled Minecraft.
I wrote something about Words with Friends 2.
At home we were getting ready for No Time to Die by watching the previous four Daniel Craig Bond films… and rating them. And then we went and saw it and I wrote a bit of a review.
Likewise, with the coming of the new Dune movie (part I) we watched the 1984 version of the tale. The new film got a bit of a review here too.
Ten Years Ago
Amazon’s game studio announced some games including the alleged MMO New World. Being given almost no information about New World did not stop some people from banging the hype drum, boosting expectations, and generally setting themselves up for disappointment. I wonder how that turned out?
Also announced was the Nintendo Switch, which would allow millennials to play video games at roof-top parties, if the trailer was to be take literally.
Civilization VI launched and became the first Civ title I did not acquire at the soonest opportunity. It just didn’t excite me. Instead I was getting my strategy game fix with Stellaris.
I reviewed the Mineserver Kickstarter campaign a year after its launch. The units were nine months late at that point, with no end to the wait in sight. The whole thing eventually failed to get off the ground. Another Kickstarter crash and burn.
I made it to level 20 in Pokemon Go. There was also a Halloween event.
Tom Chilton, of unfortunate quote fame, let out another one when he said that World of Warcraft had over 10 million subscribers again after the Legion expansion launch. Blizzard, having taken a vow of silence on subscription numbers the year before, denied everything and claimed he was mis-quoted.
Over at Daybreak they were discontinuing game cards and taking H1Z1: King of the Kill off of Station Cash as an RMT currency. They did give us firm dates for the two Kurnak based expansions for EverQuest and EverQuest II.
In EVE Online, while we were fortifying Delve our foes in the Casino War began to turn on each other, with Pandemic Legion and their followers declaring their intention to take Tribute and Vale of the Silent away from Circle of Two and TEST. All I could do was give a Nelson Muntz, “Haw-haw!” at that turn of events.
Still, that wasn’t half as much fun as CCP declaring casinos against the EULA with the coming of the Ascension expansion. Our foes would have to actually earn ISK in-game. I wondered what that would do to the economy.
We also got the YC118.9 update which, among other things, meant the death of the in-game browser. We did get breast cancer awareness skins. Yay, pink skins!
At our end of New Eden there was a lot to do. I was fighting the Blood Raider menace with my Ishtar and looking for ways to help the coalition. Reavers turned two years old and were blowing up citadels and fighting over timers in Querious. The coalition itself was ranging up into Fountain with a new doctrine.
CCP was also busy on the VR front, launching EVE Valkyrie and EVE Gunjack, the first games in the VR offensive. EVE Valkyrie was an Occulus Rift launch title FFS! All of their VR titles would sputter and fail… along with VR itself, frankly… and later be shut down, with everybody involved laid off… unless they were Icelandic citizens. They get lifetime employment.
And in World of Warcraft the Legion got its first post-launch content drop while my own enthusiasm for the expansion was starting to wane.
Finally, I was at EVE Vegas, but since it lasted through Halloween I didn’t post about it until November. Also, a new version of my blogger feed was operating in the side bar.
Fifteen Years Ago
We all said farewell to Steve Jobs.
Tobold was predicting that CCP would go bankrupt in 2012. I am NEVER EVER going to let that one go… at least not until Hilmar does the place in.
I summed up what I liked and disliked about Need for Speed: World.
I got Civilization II running on Windows 7 64-bit. People still come here for that article. I managed to get it to run on Windows 10 since then. But it didn’t work back then with my original 16-bit copy, I had to get the 32-bit version, Civilization II Gold Edition.
I started another contest, this time for Azerothian travel posters.
I recalled the start of the alien invasion!
EA was planning to unify all of its free to play online games to use the same in-game currency… something that never actually happened… also, I think all the games on the list are dead now.
Nintendo was talking about augmented reality on their new 3DS console. Five years later we got Pokemon Go… on iOS and Android.
The announcement of their Unity release got Gaff and I back to TorilMUD to mess around with the Tako Demon. I had to work to remember some MUD command syntax to get his corpse afterwards.
Then there was BlizzCon. The instance group was already bemused by Cataclysm, and the mention of Pandas did not revive our spirits. Pet Battles seemed interesting at the time. In coming to grips with the Pandaria announcements, I assumed that I would end up buying the expansion.
And then there were other WoW related things, like the announcement of the Guardian Cub, which some people predicted would be like PLEX in EVE Online. Not quite, but it probably provided test data for the eventual WoW Token idea.
In EverQuest, on the Fippy Darkpaw server, after much complaining, SOE seemed to suddenly wake up and start doing things. Problems were, you know, solved! It was becoming a kinder, gentler server. Sort of.
And then there was Rift. We started scouting it as a potential home for in instance group after the disaster in EverQuest II. The scouting went well enough that we all ended up in Telara.
Finally, I was sorting through many press releases and wondering where this so-called GDC Hall of Fame was.
Twenty Years Ago
The site got a mention in VirginWorlds Podcast episode 33 while Blessing of Kings was telling me how to be a raider in World of Warcraft.
I was defending instancing and game company forums as well as moaning about the fact that I couldn’t find a decent video card for my AGP motherboard. Also, Blizzard’s WoW patcher was pissing me off as well while Lore was mocking WoW groups. [Damn, that was done in Flash, so I guess it is gone now.]
Our Saturday night World of Warcraft instance group completed our first full dungeon run in the Deadmines. That meant my first dungeon run write up. And my second. But we got it on our third try. Then it was off to The Wailing Caverns. Did anybody have a five player dungeon adventure path like WoW back then?
I decided in EVE Online that covert ops would be a good career choice. It certainly sounds cool. However, the effort was cut short when I got to some of the pricier skills.
When it came to the then upcoming Lord of the Rings Online, I was up in arms about pointy ears and monster play, while the approaching Age of Conan made me think more about Barsoom.
I felt that fall urge to run around in EverQuest, no doubt prompted by another EQ nostalgia post, plus I wanted to take some pictures of Faydwer in order to compare them to the upcoming EverQuest II expansion, Echoes of Faydwer.
I also jumped into EverQuest II and got all confused (nothing new there) about the trade skill changes that occurred during the 10 months I was away.
And I spent some time carping about MMO pricing plans and wondering what pen and paper games might make good MMOs.
Twenty-Five Years Ago
Dark Age of Camelot launched. While I never played it… we were about to have a new baby in the house and we were having internet issues, and the world was falling apart due to 9/11… I had some friends who gave it a try. I remember it being billed as “EverQuest without the suck” at some point. Anyway, it is still alive, which is surprising because EA owned it… and still owns it, through Broadsword runs it for them.
Civilization III also showed up back in October of 2001, and I most definitely bought a copy of that. I liked a lot of the ideas it brought, but it lost some of the raw simplicity of its predecessor. I ended up playing a lot more Civ II even after Civ III was around.
Then there was Motor City Online, which was a bit of a precursor to Need for Speed: World. I am kind of sad I missed it. Of course, it was an EA MMO, so they scrapped it in less than two years, opting to go all in on The Sims Online.
Thirty Years Ago
Marathon Infinity, the last of the Marathon series of shooters from Bungie came out. That was the era of the awkwardly shaped software boxes. I owned a copy.
Most Viewed Posts in October
Out of the 20 posts on the list, only 19 and 20 were published this month. But you can see the theme for what was popular; WoW nostalgia, Enshrouded, a bit of No Man’s Sky, Pokemon Go, and a couple old favorites.
Game Time by ManicTime and Nintendo
I had eight titles with time recorded in October.
- EVE Online – 40.92%
- Over The Hill – 31.00%
- WoW Forever – 9.87%
- Stardew Valley – 8.64%
- Valheim – 4.56%
- Art of Rally – 1.73%
- Stars Reach – 1.72%
- No Man’s Sky – 1.57%
EVE Online
I spent a good chunk of my gaming time in New Eden this month, mostly pursuing the Crimson Harvest event objectives and working on that achievement to visit all of the systems in Amarr space. I finished the former… I did not get a Molok BPC sadly… and then kind of left off on the latter with 612 of 689 systems visited. I’ll get to that later.
No Man’s Sky
The start of the month saw me finishing up the Our Journey Continues expedition. But once that was done I moved on to other things… though we did get the Forsaken update just this week. I did briefly peek in on that.
Over the Hill / Art of Rally
Somewhat unexpected, Over the Hill showed up and gave Potshot and I something to fiddle with while waiting for WoW Forever to arrive. It is a simple yet fulfilling title which clearly ate up some time. I also reinstalled Art of Rally just to take a look at the previous Funselektor driving game. I am much better at off road objectives that don’t have a timer than rally racing, that is for sure. But I’ll get to that.
Pokemon Go
You’d think I could have gotten three more max battles this month… and I would have been there had I been willing to use the cash shop to unlock the artificial limits imposed by the Saudis… why is it always them? Anyway, that will be done in November for sure.
- Level: 76
- XP Progress: 97.5% of the 203,353,000 xp needed for level 80
- Tasks for Level 77
  - XP: DONE
  - Platinum Medals: 41 of 41- DONE
  - Power up 7 Pokemon to their max CP: 7 of 7 – DONE
  - Win 100 Max Battles: 97 of 100
  - Make 10 trades with Pokemon caught at least 300km apart: 10 of 10 – DONE
- Pokedex status: 944 (+4) caught
- Pokemon I want: Phione, Manaphy, and Arceus, none of which have been released yet
- Current buddy: Swapping between Pikachu buddies to get candies for another max CP
Stardew Valley
My daughter and I have carried on, though we missed a weekend here and there due to travel, work, and school. Still, we try to get together to play when we can.
Stars Reach
Playable Worlds has been pushing hard to get people to log in, holding events every weekend, though that hasn’t seemed to boost their numbers anywhere close to where things need to be for financial success. I dropped in a couple of times, though not during events due to time conflicts, and found very little that interested me. Builders have grabbed land around the portals on the few planets, outside of which is the desolation zone where they have strip mined, which was a predictable outcome. I ended up uninstalling the game. Maybe something interesting will arrive at some future date.
Valheim
I have been lightly playing Valheim since it hit 1.0 last month. There was something wrong with the original world I started off with, so spawned a new world with a different seed where things seemed to be going better. The exploration bug seemed to be satisfied more so with Over the Hill in the back half of the month, but I’ll get back to Valheim I am sure.
WoW Forever
I did not play as much of the beta as I thought I would, but I played enough to sell me on the whole idea. It is fine. We’ll see how it ends up going once it launches.
Coming Up
Kind of a big month coming up.
Probably the biggest video game news will be the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. Since it will be on consoles only initially, and since I barely started GTA V… 98 minutes played back in 2019… that will likely be a non-event for me.
And for Nintendo peeps, there is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time coming in November as well. I think this video sums up the tension between the two launches pretty well.
More on my front, we will see WoW Forever go live next week. That should be comedy and chaos for at least a week as Blizz tries to deal with the onslaught of new players, old players, sight seers, bots, gold farmers, and RMT spammers trying to rush the gates.
Back in 2019 I declared that first day login issues and the like were a problem the industry was never going to solve. We now have the most popular, well funded MMORPG studio poised to test that thesis. They know what is coming. Can they prove me wrong? And will it really matter if it all settles down in a week or so anyway? We shall see!
EVE Online also has the Fractured Skies expansion coming out on November 10th. Expect them to throw some free game time and have login rewards to entice people to try out their new stuff. While PC MMOs probably don’t have much to fear from GTA VI, CCP/Fenris trying to soft launch, early access, paid alpha test EVE Vanguard within a week of that does feel like folly. But there was never going to be a good time to do that, now was there?
Finally, the US has a big mid-term election on Tuesday where only voter fraud and blatant electoral interference should save the Republicans. Can their evil malice overcome their stunning incompetence? We shall see.

results.title: Hackers hijack Egypt highway billboard and Malaysian screens to show porn
results.author: Saher
results.content:
A hacking group claiming responsibility for displaying pornographic footage on a roadside billboard in Egypt told The Cairo Report that it exploited a software vulnerability affecting digital advertising screens in several countries, exposing what it described as widespread security failures in commercially operated infrastructure.
The group, which operates a Telegram channel called ‘Leakers$’, said its members discovered thousands of exposed systems through an automated scan lasting approximately two hours, during which it identified Iraq, Malaysia, Brazil, and China among the countries where it said it gained access to display systems.
The account follows an incident Thursday, Oct. 29, when sexually explicit footage appeared on a large electronic billboard overlooking one of the busiest highways in the country, the 26 July Corridor in Giza, which connects Cairo with its western suburbs.
Videos circulated on social media showed the footage playing on the screen, prompting authorities to suspend advertising displays along the road and open an investigation.
The affected billboard is operated by Arabian United, an Egyptian-Saudi advertising venture established by United Media Services (UMS), Egypt’s intelligence-linked media conglomerate, and Saudi-listed Arabian Contracting Services Co.
In a statement Thursday evening, Egypt’s Interior Ministry attributed the incident to the hacking of an unnamed international advertising company’s website, saying the same footage had appeared on screens in several countries simultaneously.
The ministry did not identify the international company, the countries affected, or any suspects. It also gave no technical explanation of how the alleged website breach translated into control over roadside advertising displays.
The group’s account broadly supports the ministry’s description of an international incident but provides a different level of technical detail.
In an exchange with The Cairo Report, a person speaking on behalf of the group said its members had exploited a vulnerability in the software used to transmit content to LED displays, rather than targeting the Egyptian billboard individually.
“It was a genuine vulnerability in the software responsible for transmitting content to LED displays,” the person said. “After exploiting it, we gained access to display systems in several countries, not just Egypt, but also Malaysia, Brazil, China, and others.”
The person added that the infrastructure was not exclusive to Egypt and contained multiple security flaws, including weaknesses accessible through the system’s own pages and interfaces.
Asked whether the operation involved exploiting an unknown software vulnerability or merely accessing poorly protected equipment exposed to the public internet, the representative described a software flaw but did not provide enough technical evidence to establish the precise method.
According to the representative, the group located its targets through automated scanning rather than selecting particular companies or countries.
“The systems were identified through an automated and random scan,” they said, adding that several participants using the online pseudonyms Never, 19ylegal, CH and Nivex were involved in identifying thousands of exposed systems over approximately two hours.
The representative shared visual records captured during the incident and referred to material on the group’s public Telegram channel.
The channel’s address was visible on the pornographic material displayed on the Egyptian billboard, allowing The Cairo Report to trace it and contact its administrators.
In its initial public statement, the group said its objective was to expose security failures rather than demand payment or carry out a ransomware attack.
“Companies charge millions to build infrastructure across multiple countries and leave LED screens and billboard networks wide open on the internet without basic protection,” the statement said.
The group also rejected the idea that taking control of the screens required advanced technical capabilities.
“It wasn’t nearly as complex an operation as many might imagine,” its representative told The Cairo Report.
Perhaps most importantly, the intrusion raises questions about cybersecurity oversight at Arabian United, whose shareholders include one of the Egyptian state’s most politically influential media companies.
UMS, the media arm of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service, was established in 2016 and controls more than 40 companies across television, newspapers, digital media, entertainment, and advertising.
The billboard’s operator, Arabian United, however, was established in 2022 through a partnership between UMS and Arabian Contracting Services Co., one of Saudi Arabia’s largest outdoor advertising businesses.
According to the Saudi company’s 2025 annual report, its Egyptian subsidiary operates a network of 1,926 advertising billboards, including 239 digital installations, across Cairo, Giza, Alexandria and the North Coast.
The Saudi company holds a 49.99% ownership stake in Arabian United but exercises effective corporate control through its 57% representation on the board of directors, according to its March 2026 financial statements.
The company’s annual report also says it supervises, manages, and operates every stage of the advertising process in Egypt, from installing screens and securing advertising clients to displaying their content.
That division of responsibilities is significant because the Interior Ministry attributed the incident to an “international service provider” without identifying it or explaining its contractual relationship with the Egyptian operator.
When asked what the incident suggested about the security capabilities of an advertising business associated with Egyptian intelligence, the group’s representative said such institutional connections offered no guarantee against technical weaknesses.
“If infrastructure operated by a company linked to Egyptian intelligence can be compromised, it demonstrates that such connections do not necessarily translate into strong cybersecurity,” the representative said.
Obviously, the association with UMS does not establish that Egyptian intelligence agencies were responsible for administering the compromised systems. It does, however, place the incident within a security apparatus-linked commercial network that has expanded its presence across some of Egypt’s most heavily monitored public spaces.
Arabian United acknowledged the intrusion, saying an unknown party had gained unauthorized access to one of its advertising screens.
The company said it had immediately suspended the screen, was investigating the incident in coordination with authorities, and that it “remained committed to the highest security and operating standards.”
Earlier in the day, security sources told Al-Shorouk that investigators were “examining whether the footage resulted from an external intrusion or had been uploaded by someone responsible for operating the screen.”
The incident also exposes a gap between the government’s extensive regulation of roadside advertising content and the publicly disclosed safeguards governing the digital systems on which that advertising increasingly depends.
Under Law No. 208 of 2020, Egypt established the National Authority for the Regulation of Roadside Advertising, reporting to the prime minister. Its board includes representatives of the defense, interior, and transport ministries, among other government bodies.
The authority is responsible for setting standards governing roadside advertising, including requirements concerning “public order and morality.”
At a September 2025 meeting, prime minister Mostafa Madbouly emphasized the need to “regulate advertising on public roads,” particularly “compliance with Egyptian societal values and the protection of the urban landscape.”
Neither that regulatory framework nor the government’s latest statements explain what cybersecurity standards apply to remotely operated advertising networks, whether the affected operator had undergone a security assessment, or who bears responsibility for auditing third-party software connected to publicly visible screens.
The Interior Ministry said legal procedures had been initiated but did not specify whether the investigation would examine failures by the Egyptian operator or its contractors.

### Key Points
- The hacking group, known as ‘Leakers$’, claimed to have identified thousands of exposed digital advertising systems globally through automated scans.
- The incident occurred on the 26 July Corridor in Giza, involving a billboard operated by Arabian United, a joint venture between United Media Services and Arabian Contracting Services.
- Egypt’s Interior Ministry confirmed the breach, attributing the incident to the hacking of an unnamed international advertising company’s website.
- The hackers reported gaining unauthorized access to display systems in multiple countries, including Iraq, Malaysia, Brazil, and China.
- Arabian United operates a network of 1,926 billboards in Egypt, including 239 digital installations, and has suspended the affected screen pending an investigation.

### Why it Matters
- This breach highlights significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities within the rapidly expanding digital infrastructure of public advertising networks. It raises urgent questions regarding the oversight of third-party software and the lack of standardized security protocols for systems operating in highly visible public spaces.

results.title: Spam Guide Update, Restaurant Controls & AI Mode Revenue – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
results.author: Matt G. Southern
results.content:
Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates have an impact on which user-created pages are meant for Search, who is able to turn off ordering links on restaurant profiles, and just how much to read into a page-indexing report that appears to no longer update.
Google added information about indexing shareable pages to its spam guide and provided restaurants with direct control over ordering providers. In response to a user’s report that their page-indexing data was no longer updating, John Mueller at Google referred to the date on the reports. New citation data and Alphabet’s earnings round out the week.
Here’s what matters for you and your work.
Google’s Spam Guide Adds Indexing Advice For Shareable Pages
In a section added Oct. 26, Google’s guide to preventing user-generated spam now recommends that platforms, by default, apply noindex or block crawling on pages created for direct sharing.
Key facts:
The new part, “Only index content meant for Search,” is concerned with webpages that were designed “for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery.” There are two options for this type of webpage; using the noindex (via a robots meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag HTTP header), or adding a crawl-block in your robots.txt file. Google now recommends you confirm your website in Search Console to receive notifications of manual actions and security issues, and also check your Page Indexing and Search performance reports to see if there have been “unexpected spikes.” Neither the guide nor the changelog mentions any changes in how Google will enforce these guidelines.
Why This Matters
Robots.txt will stop Google from crawling the pages it blocks, however according to Google’s introduction to robots.txt, the file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Even though a URL has been disallowed in robots.txt, that does not mean Google cannot find it; as long as another site links to your URL it may appear in search results. A noindex rule will prevent share link URLs or generated page URLs you wish to remove from appearing in search engine results only if Googlebot can crawl and read them.
Read our full coverage: Google Updates Spam Guide For Shared Pages, Generated Content & Apps and Google Signals A Wider Crackdown On SEO Spam
Restaurants Can Now Turn Off Ordering Providers In Business Profile
Restaurants can now turn off specific third-party ordering providers directly from their Google Business Profile dashboard, Google’s Lisa Landsman wrote on LinkedIn on Oct. 28.
Key facts:
The post included a screenshot of the individual pickup and delivery buttons under “Show provider to customers.” When asked about which countries allow the feature, product manager at Google, Michael G. stated that all do. Prior to this, restaurants were able to submit a removal request on a provider through their Business Profile; however, the provider was required to complete the action, and Google’s help page gives providers up to 5 business days after a request to remove the link.
Why This Matters
Google’s policy page for ordering providers says “All partner integrations are enabled by default.” It’s worth checking the ordering list on each restaurant profile you manage to make sure it doesn’t include providers the restaurant doesn’t use.
Read our full coverage: Google Gives Restaurants Direct Control Over Ordering Providers
Mueller Points To Report Dates When Asked About Stale Indexing Data
A user on a social media site, Reddit, stated they had not received an update of their Page indexing report since Oct. 16 and questioned if this was due to some type of stall in the data pipeline. In response to this question, John Mueller from Google said, “I don’t think it makes sense for me / us to comment on the data freshness for all reports all the time, this is why we put dates in there.”
Key facts:
Mueller stated that this user’s website appeared to be fairly recent and had steady numbers; he added “Indexing doesn’t change quickly, and when it does, you see that reflected in the performance reports first.” Mueller told the user to “save your energy,” and that Google focuses on faster updates “where we think it’s actually useful for folks.” Mueller did not indicate if the report was late. On Oct. 29, I checked SEJ’s property in the page indexing report, which indicated the most recent data update was Oct. 22.
Why This Matters
Before interpreting a drop or rise in indexed pages, it’s worth checking the Page indexing report’s last-update date, as the chart may lag behind what’s happening on your site. Mueller’s reply points to the Performance report as the first place to look for indexing changes.
Read our full coverage: Google Responds To Concern Over Search Console Indexing Reports
AI-Cited Pages More Often Opened With A Direct Answer, Agency Data Shows
TJ Robertson analyzed 193,507 AI answers from ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and AI Overviews. In two rounds of blind ratings, the analysis found that cited pages more often opened with a direct answer to the question than the comparison pages did.
Key facts:
In comparison to pages that came up for the same answer to users’ questions but were not cited, cited pages directly answered user queries in their opening lines in 23%, while the uncited pages did so in 14%. In comparison to Google’s top 10 results that the AI never pulled up, the split was 20% for cited pages versus 5% for those top 10 pages on all 195 rated pairs. These statistics were taken from questions tracked by Robertson’s agency TJ Digital for their clients, and TJ Digital sells both SEO and generative engine optimization services. Robertson states that he has identified association (not causation), not proof that a particular feature of a webpage causes it to be referenced.
Why This Matters
When the pages that were not referenced had also come up in the AI’s search, this gap in opening answers given on a page (both for reference and non-reference pages) was smaller. Seeing if the key pages answer the question in the first line will give you a good fast check, and you can compare these patterns with those of the questions you are tracking.
Read our full coverage: AI-Cited Pages More Often Got Straight To The Answer
Google Says Lower AI Mode Monetization Weighed On Search Growth
Alphabet’s third-quarter results show Google Search & other revenue rising 12% year over year to $63.35 billion, following growth of 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2.
Key facts:
Asked on the earnings call whether fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode explained slower Search growth, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler named currency as the biggest factor in the slowdown from Q2, then developments in retail and media. He then said “the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” and added, “To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here.” The same day, Google expanded ads in AI Mode to 10 more countries and said it’s launching multiturn ads in the U.S.
Why This Matters
Schindler didn’t say what AI Mode monetization was lower than, or by how much. Neither Pichai’s published Q3 remarks nor the call included a figure for clicks sent to websites, which he gave in Q2, so the quarter adds detail on AI Mode revenue and none on that traffic.
Read our full coverage: Google Says Lower AI Mode Monetization Weighed On Search Growth
Theme Of The Week: The Check Is Yours To Run
This week’s updates include defaults, date stamps, and caveats. Defaults shape what people see until someone chooses to change them, from the indexing setting on a share page to the ordering providers on a restaurant profile. The date stamps and caveats, on a Search Console report, a set of citation data and Alphabet’s earnings, mark the limit of what each source told you. What happened on your own sites is the check left for you to run.
Top Stories Of The Week:
More Resources:
- Google Reports Search Console Page Indexing Report Delays
- Google On Robots.txt: When To Use Noindex vs. Disallow
- Google Search Revenue Growth Eases After A Year Of Acceleration
Featured Image: Cast Of Thousands/Shutterstock

### Key Points

results.title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
results.author: Ryan Fetterman
results.content:
- VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.
- If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.
- This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.
There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.
After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.
The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.
The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”
VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.
| Endpoint | https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions | 
| Default model | anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 | 
| Fallback chain | moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash | 
| Temperature | 0.2 — deterministic, consistent output | 
| Request format | Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 | 
Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.
The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.
The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.
Stealer capabilities
VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.
Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.
What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.
After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.
The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.
Deployment model
Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.
This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.
If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.
All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.
Countermeasures
Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. 
In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.
Conclusions
VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.
The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.
The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.
Sample details
| SHA256 | 57ef4242666d78c50df145b34023df564f0fad38812d6a580e66433d427e2279 | 
| Filename | 9BY0tjwOc3ut.exe / yLP9m5J3i2Aw.exe | 
| Type | PE32+ x86-64 | 
| PE Timestamp | 2026-08-17 20:35 | 
| First Seen (UTC) | 2026-10-11 12:46 |
results.summary:
The new VOLTA-AUTODOXER malware uses integrated artificial intelligence to analyze stolen victim data, automatically ranking the monetization value of compromised credentials and personal information for cybercriminals.

### Key Points
- VOLTA-AUTODOXER is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that harvests browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, session tokens, and personal metadata.
- The malware uses a multi-model LLM architecture, including Claude, Kimi, and Gemini, to act as a forensic analyst that prioritizes high-value targets.
- It performs live enrichment by using stolen session tokens to query services like Gmail, UberEats, and DoorDash to confirm home addresses and financial details.
- The tool operates without attacker-owned infrastructure, instead utilizing third-party APIs like OpenRouter to process and structure stolen data into a "dossier."
- A builder-style distribution model allows customers to compile custom binaries, shifting the burden of manual data analysis from the attacker to the AI.

### Why it Matters
This development marks a shift in cybercrime where AI is used to automate the labor-intensive process of triaging stolen data, effectively lowering the barrier for attackers to identify high-value victims. By turning raw logs into actionable intelligence, this malware allows even unsophisticated operators to scale their operations and maximize the financial return on every compromise.

results.title: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?
results.author: Dave Vellante
results.content:
Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?
The artificial intelligence buildout is making an enormous bet on what businesses will eventually be willing to pay for intelligence. In our research this summer on forecasting the AI bubble, we argued that a key indicator to watch is productive utilization by enterprise customers.
Specifically, we said at the time, if infrastructure supply catches up before productive monetization materializes, the risk of a bubble popping increases to what we felt were dangerous levels. We forecast that the supply constraints and healthy capital funding appetites at that time could provide conditions for a soft landing. And we pegged 2029 as the highest-risk year.
And that brings us to the next obvious question: What has to happen inside mainstream enterprises for their AI investments to become economically self-funding? Michael Burry’s analysis of Anthropic PBC highlights the scale and interconnectedness of the commitments that Anthropic is making. Apollo’s research by Torsten Slok raises questions about how broadly the financial benefits are showing up today. And the history of the personal computer and internet eras reminds us that productivity gains aren’t always immediate, and that powerful technologies can coexist with what initially seem to be poor investment returns that take time to appear.
We think the path to a soft landing runs through changes in how businesses operate, specifically the work that they do, the people that they need, how they scale and the value that their customers are ultimately going to pay for. Welcome to Breaking Analysis, episode 332: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?
Joining us today is Crawford Del Prete. He’s the former president of IDC and now senior adviser at PSG Equity. For decades, Crawford has had a front-row seat on technology transitions, and he brings current perspectives on how software businesses are adapting to AI, how new AI-native companies are forming, and what the emerging operating model looks like. Crawford, welcome. Good to see you.
Crawford Del Prete: Hey, great to see you, Dave.
Where AI is changing economics
Dave Vellante: As of this recording, the Nasdaq is down almost 1,000 points, so it’s getting worse by the minute. It’s not quite at 1,000, it’s only down 937. There are a lot of reasons there. Of course, we had earnings last night from the big hyperscalers which were not well received.
Google’s disappointment in advertising and AWS’ capex spend and negative cash flow were the culprits, but the hyperscalers are cranking in cloud. Anyway, let’s start with what you’re seeing, specifically in the market, but also inside businesses. Where is AI changing economics from your point of view?
Crawford Del Prete: Well, AI is changing economics in so many different areas, right? So we’re starting to see the early signs of productivity gains, but we’re not yet seeing them in the numbers. And what I’m seeing is that companies are starting to automate workflows. They’re starting to use AI in different ways. And those ways are ways that you would expect initially, right? So we saw a big move toward coding. We saw a big move toward customer service. But now we’re starting to get into a lot of the other areas where individual tasks are starting to get automated within organizations.
And as that happens, it becomes very uneven in terms of how we’re starting to see the impact of AI in organizations on an everyday basis. Again, jobs are made up of hundreds, sometimes thousands of tasks. And now we’re starting to automate those tasks, but we haven’t necessarily changed the way work is wired in an organization. So I think that makes for some of the inconsistencies that I think we’ll talk about in a minute in terms of the productivity numbers that we’re seeing.
Funding the AI buildout
Dave Vellante: Thank you for that. You and I cut our teeth during the PC era. And of course, we learned Moore’s Law was everything. We learned about the rapidly declining prices. Tech was always deflationary. Now tech is inflationary. Remember, you and I used to follow the disk drive markets, and customers would want to lock in. They’d want to have a forward pricing contract.
Crawford Del Prete: Yes.
Dave Vellante: Historic declines followed a curve according to Moore’s Law. Today you want to lock in current prices because they’re going up. So you’re seeing all kinds of crazy dislocations. The Anthropic S-1 came out this week, and there were definitely some positive numbers in the document. Everybody, of course, talks about the revenue growth. We’ve never seen anything like it before: 14x in the first half of 2026 to $16 billion. But what really stood out to me, Crawford, was the balance sheet. The company says they’ve got $132 billion in liquid assets, so cash and equivalents. And there are only two nonbanks in the U.S. — and this has been reported — that have more cash than Anthropic. That’s, of course, Alphabet and Berkshire.
And remember, they’ve raised about $140 billion. So let that sink in for the audience a bit. It basically has burned $10 billion to get to a $32 billion revenue run rate. But the big question, of course, is around the economic return on that capacity that’s being committed.
Michael Burry, who writes Cassandra Unchained — his work, by the way, is unparalleled. His ideas are often pooh-poohed. He got sort of slammed for the whole GPU lifecycle, and people dismiss him, but his research is deep and unique. And this diagram shows the interconnected financing and commercial relationships around Anthropic. He pulled this all together from the S-1, and you see it’s $537 billion of multiyear compute commitments across all kinds of different arrangements. You’ve got take-or-pay deals, minimum purchase agreements, lease deals, capacity that’s conditioned upon delivery, stuff like that. Of course, this isn’t current debt, but it’s stuff that they’ve committed to.
So Crawford, I’ve got a bunch of questions for you. Just answer them all, or whatever you have best visibility on. First of all, you’ve got capital providers and infrastructure suppliers and model companies. They’re all sort of interconnected. So how much of a concern is that? Are your portfolio companies spending more? Is it because AI is showing better return, or is it because they have FOMO and they’ve gotta remain competitive? And of course, your new startups are going like a rocket ship and growing with less labor, and they potentially show us the way to the future. What are your thoughts on all that?
Crawford Del Prete: So look, Dave, you and I have been around this industry forever, and we’ve never been at a point where you’ve got an interconnected industry that is built on yesterday’s architecture because a new architecture that came along had to be redefined. And so once it was redefined, it had to be built. And so you’ve connected the world, and now you’ve said, well, the stack that you had was the wrong stack. So we’re going to have to build a new stack, and that new stack is going to create applications and usage that will immediately be at 100% capacity.
So this circular financing is, in my opinion, a way to basically rebuild the stack around the world all at the same time. And so you ask the question: What are we seeing in terms of demand from end-user customers? And I would tell you, it’s an unsatisfying answer, but it depends on the customer, right?
So I talked to one customer this week that said to me, “I cannot get my hands on enough compute capacity.” And I pushed back and said, “Wait a minute.” “No, no, no, you don’t understand. All the capacity that I could buy from a Lenovo, all the capacity I could buy from an HPE, from a Dell — I’ll take it all.” And so they’re willing to get as much as an OEM is willing to give them. And these are obviously very, very quantitative-oriented customers. But again, the demand in a lot of these places is truly insatiable.
Other customers are starting to look at token spend. And what I’m seeing in those customers — and this will ring very, very true to things that you and I developed 25 years ago — they’re looking at workloads, and they’re starting to look at AI workloads, and they’re starting to teach people to say, “Hey, you know what? That Opus 4.8 model, not a very bad model. Probably don’t need to use the 5.0 on the extra effort and peel through six times as many tokens.” So they’re starting to agitate models for specific workloads.
And so we’re kind of at the beginning of that journey with customers, but I’ll tell you, this is going to look just like you and I looked at the server market back 20 years ago, where eventually you’re going to have different models for different workloads, and that’s going to include open-source and open-weight models that are inside of a data center or inside of a cloud. The reality is, it’s all over the map. But I will tell you that I’m not seeing tons of customers saying, “I’ve got to pull back,” because it’s about competitiveness. I’ve got to be competitive, and I’ve got to give my team members the tools to achieve things they never could achieve before with AI.
Dave Vellante: We did slice the workload salami pretty thin at IDC, didn’t we? And to your point about this whole new architecture you’re seeing at Intel today, Intel’s down 30% today.
Crawford Del Prete: Yes.
Dave Vellante: Basically, general-purpose x86 is kind of being absorbed into accelerated computing. I guess PCs are obviously what folks missed. I don’t know how they missed it, but Intel doesn’t really have a strong position in GPUs. And AMD is eating away at its market share in PCs. And so that’s a real conundrum. In your quant example, that customer’s monetizing, right? That’s why they want as much compute as possible, right?
Crawford Del Prete: That customer is monetizing all day long and is saying, “Look, I can innovate by giving my users more capacity, and they can do things they never could do before. They can create analysis. They can create deliverables that they never were able to create before.” And so I would say that those kinds of customers exist, and they exist at scale. And I feel like there is not this big dichotomy between customers in terms of who’s willing to spend and who’s not willing to spend. Everybody’s willing to spend. It really just comes down to the amount of resources that they have.
Now, you asked the second question, which is: Are companies spending more because AI is improving their economics, or because they have to do it to remain competitive? And I will tell you that whether it’s a portfolio company or it’s not, there is no software company today that is not investing for AI. They have to. They’ve got to do it to increase their product set to be competitive, because there are many, many competitive factors that never existed before. And these are all things that I’m looking at every single day.
There’s a whole discussion around: Can an adjacent, large, at-scale platform, by using AI, absorb your area, the area you’re innovating in? And then separately, there’s the omnipresent question of — and we can talk about this for a while — can customers vibe code? And can they create a software product as opposed to licensing it or using it? So everybody is investing. And if you’re not investing in AI — there are a few companies in that category, but very, very few — then you’re probably writing your own death sentence.
Dave Vellante: Right. And you, as a capital allocator, aren’t that interested in investing in a company that’s not investing in AI.
Crawford Del Prete: Exactly.
From individual productivity to business results
Dave Vellante: Okay, so we’re going to try to square this circle, because we see these relationships that Anthropic and others have struck, how they’re funding the buildout. But our premise today is that the viability of those ultimately is going to depend on what value end customers can create from that capacity. Crawford just laid out that they can’t get enough compute, so that’s somewhat of a blocker. I would throw in governance, with all the surveys that we do around governance. People are afraid of AI. They’re worried about security.
Now, last weekend, Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok put forth his view of how far those benefits, the AI benefits, have spread. So he compared inflation-adjusted revenue per employee at the Mag Seven, which is that top line that’s going up, with the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. And you can see that top line pulling away. It was showing increases from around $600,000 per employee, which is pretty good, in 2023 to about $800,000 today. And then that broader group is kind of flattish. And his point is that AI hasn’t, at least, shown up broadly.
He also went on in the piece to point to the lack of productivity gains and highlighted the circular financing concerns. We’re going to talk about the J-curve in a moment, but I know you read that Apollo post.
Crawford Del Prete: Right.
Dave Vellante: How does it fit with what you were saying earlier inside of businesses? Are the gains kind of narrowly confined? You mentioned the quant company. You mentioned broadly everybody has FOMO.
